newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge commander says hostages in good health.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge commander says hostages in good health.

text.p: Feared hardline Khmer Rouge commander Ta Mok told senior Cambodian military officers on Monday that 15 government officials who have been unable to leave his territory were in good health.

"The 15 officials are very well," Lieutenant General Meas Sophea told Reuters after returning to Phnom Penh from the northwest province of Siem Reap, where he and other senior officers had talked with the one-legged Ta Mok by radio link.

Second Prime Minister Hun Sen said last week the 15 were being held hostage, but First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said the next day they were negotiating the defection of hardliners and were not being held against their will.

Cambodia's armed forces deputy chief of staff said there had been no progress on securing the release of the 15, including Siem Reap Deputy Governor Hem Bunheng, but said no conditions had been mentioned. He gave no more details on the talks.

They flew to rebel territory on February 14 and never returned from their mission to win over more Khmer Rouge defectors. Some fear they are being used to win leverage in negotiations for more defections.
Ranariddh was optimistic when asked about the negotiators on Monday, saying he expected their return.

Some analysts interpreted the conflicting information from the co-premiers as a sign of renewed tension between them over the defections from the Khmer Rouge, which led the brutal 1975-1979 "killing fields" regime.
More than a million Cambodians were either murdered as suspected enemies of the Khmer Rouge regime or died from overwork or lack of health care.

The premiers, who formed an uneasy coalition after U.N.-run polls in 1993, have vied to win over defectors to their rival parties since the guerrilla movement began crumbling last August and continue to differ over how to handle the ex-Khmer Rouge.

But analysts said the participation of Meas Sophea, a member of Hun Sen's Cambodian People Party, in the talks with Ta Mok was a positive sign of cooperation as the prince's FUNCINPEC had been talking with the hardliners on their own.
The Khmer Rouge signed a U.N.-sponsored peace pact in 1991 but later reneged on the deal and have been fighting the coalition elected in 1993.
Fewer than 2,000 fighters are believed to remain in the hardliners' northern base of Anlong Veng, including Ta Mok.
